questions.stem: An adult with suspected infection has a MAP of 58 mm Hg, mottled skin, altered mentation, and lactate 4.8 mmol/L. Septic shock is strongly suspected. Which action best reflects the current Surviving Sepsis Campaign approach?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Wait for final culture identification before starting antimicrobials so therapy can be narrowed from the first dose and unnecessary broad coverage is avoided.","B":"Begin sepsis resuscitation immediately, obtain cultures before antimicrobials when feasible, measure lactate, and give antimicrobials without avoidable delay.","C":"Delay antimicrobials for up to three hours because rapid diagnostic assessment should precede treatment even when the patient has clinical evidence of septic shock.","D":"Give a fixed 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus before individual assessment because the guideline treats this volume as a mandatory first step for suspected infection."}}
questions.rationale: Sepsis and septic shock are medical emergencies. The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends blood cultures as soon as possible and ideally before antimicrobials, lactate measurement, immediate resuscitation, and immediate antimicrobial therapy for septic shock, ideally within 1 hour. The suggested 30 mL/kg initial crystalloid volume applies to sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock in the first 3 hours and requires ongoing reassessment rather than automatic use in every suspected infection.
questions.source_name: Society of Critical Care Medicine — Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026
questions.source_detail: 2026 adult guideline: cultures ASAP ideally before antimicrobials; measure lactate; sepsis/septic shock treatment begins immediately; septic shock antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 hour; fluids individualized and reassessed.

questions.stem: Immediately before incision for a spinal procedure, the circulating nurse finds that the signed consent lists the left side but the operating-room schedule lists the right side. What should the team do?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Proceed because the signed consent is the controlling document, and correct the operating-room schedule after the procedure is completed and documented.","B":"Ask the surgeon privately which side is intended, then proceed if the surgeon confirms the left side without repeating verification with the full procedure team.","C":"Stop progression toward incision and resolve the discrepancy through the preprocedure verification process and final team time-out before the procedure begins.","D":"Rely on the site mark alone because a visible mark replaces the need to reconcile conflicting documents during the final verification process."}}
questions.rationale: The Universal Protocol requires discrepancies to be reconciled before the procedure proceeds. The final time-out immediately before incision uses active team communication to verify the correct patient, procedure, and site; one clinician's private confirmation or a single document does not replace team verification.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — Universal Protocol / Final Time-Out
questions.source_detail: Current Universal Protocol guidance requires final verification with the immediate procedure team and reconciliation of discrepancies before the procedure begins.

questions.stem: An older adult admitted with acute confusion cannot name home medications. The spouse brings medication bottles, and the community pharmacy can provide dispensing records. What is the safest admission approach?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Enter the medications the client can personally name and defer outside-source verification because family and pharmacy information may conflict with the client's recollection.","B":"Continue medications found in the brought-in bottles unless an admission order explicitly discontinues them, because possession suggests they remain part of the regimen.","C":"Delay medication reconciliation until discharge because admission orders should be based on the acute diagnosis rather than the outpatient medication history.","D":"Create the best possible medication list from reliable sources, compare it with current orders, and resolve and document discrepancies before the regimen is finalized."}}
questions.rationale: Medication reconciliation requires building the best possible current medication list from reliable available sources, comparing that list with admission orders, and resolving discrepancies. Relying only on the confused client's recall, blindly continuing bottles, or waiting until discharge creates avoidable omission, duplication, and interaction risk.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — Effectively Managing Medications
questions.source_detail: Medication reconciliation is a transition-of-care safety process intended to maintain and communicate accurate medication information and resolve discrepancies.

questions.stem: Two hospitalized clients with the same last name are in adjacent rooms. Before administering a high-alert medication, which identification method is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use at least two person-specific identifiers, such as full name and date of birth, and match them with the medication record before administration.","B":"Use the room number and last name because the combination identifies the client reliably when the rooms and assignments were recently confirmed.","C":"Ask another nurse to visually identify the client because recognition by a staff member is an acceptable substitute for two patient identifiers.","D":"Use the client's diagnosis and bed location because clinical information is more specific than demographic identifiers during medication administration."}}
questions.rationale: The Joint Commission requires at least two person-specific identifiers when providing care, treatment, or services. A room number or physical location is not an acceptable patient identifier. Matching two identifiers to the medication record reduces wrong-patient error risk.
questions.source_detail: Use at least two person-specific identifiers; room number or physical location is not an acceptable unique patient identifier.

questions.stem: After a near miss involving hydrOXYzine and hydrALAZINE, the medication-safety team reviews storage and labeling. Which change best addresses this risk?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Remind nurses to memorize the spelling difference and leave the medications together because experienced clinicians should distinguish similar names without system changes.","B":"Separate the look-alike medications, use approved name-differentiation strategies and barcode safeguards, and review storage and labeling for additional risk reduction.","C":"Remove barcode scanning for these medications because scanning can distract staff from reading labels and increases reliance on automated identification systems.","D":"Store the medications alphabetically in the same bin and add a general warning sign because consistent alphabetic placement is the strongest defense against name confusion."}}
questions.rationale: HydrOXYzine and hydrALAZINE are a classic look-alike/sound-alike risk. Medication-safety design uses system defenses such as name differentiation, separation where appropriate, barcode verification, and review of packaging/storage rather than relying on memory alone.
questions.source_name: Institute for Safe Medication Practices — Confused Drug Names
questions.source_detail: ISMP maintains resources for confused drug names and recommends system-level risk-reduction strategies such as name differentiation and safer storage/verification practices.
